title: 3Sum
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every triplet with a dedup set versus sorting and a two pointer search.

blocks.text: Given an array nums, return all unique triplets [nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]] such that the three indices are distinct and the three values sum to 0. The answer must not contain duplicate triplets.

blocks.title: Analogy: Balancing a Three Way Scale
blocks.text: Like searching a bag of positive and negative weights for any three that balance a scale perfectly at zero, one weight pulling one way and the others balancing it out, without picking the same physical weight twice.

blocks.caption: Find every unique triplet of values that adds up to zero

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Only positive values and one zero are present","no combination of three can reach a sum of 0","every value is 0 or positive, so any three chosen sum to at least 0 and can only equal 0 if all three are 0, which they are not"],["Answer","empty list","no valid triplet exists"]]}

blocks.text: All three zeros together sum to 0, and since they are the only values available, the answer is a single triplet: [[0, 0, 0]].
It helps to ask what specifically makes finding triplets harder than finding pairs, and what tool removes that extra difficulty.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Two Sum solved the pair version of this question with a hash map lookup for a complement, in a single pass with no sorting needed.

Observation 2: Nesting that same hash map idea inside an outer loop over a fixed first value would reduce 3Sum to n separate 2Sum calls, but on an unsorted array, catching duplicate triplets in the output still requires an extra set, exactly what the brute force resorts to.

Observation 3: Sorting the array first removes that awkwardness directly. Once sorted, any repeated value sits immediately next to its duplicates, so skipping "same value as just before" is a single cheap comparison instead of a whole extra data structure.

Observation 4: Sorting also unlocks a second benefit for free: with the fixed value chosen, finding a pair in the remaining sorted slice that sums to its negation is exactly the two pointer pattern already used in Valid Palindrome, one pointer at each end, moving inward based on whether the current sum is too small or too large.
Sorting is the single decision that both simplifies duplicate handling and unlocks the two pointer search, which is why it comes before anything else in the optimized approach.
Check every possible combination of three distinct indices, and whenever their values sum to zero, record that triplet after sorting it, using a set to avoid storing the same triplet twice.

items: For every triple of indices i, j, k with i less than j less than k, check whether nums[i] plus nums[j] plus nums[k] equals 0.
If it does, sort the three values and add them to a set of found triplets, so duplicates collapse automatically.
Convert the set back to a list at the end.

codes.python:
def three_sum(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    found = set()
    for i in range(n):                                      # try every first index
        for j in range(i + 1, n):                              # try every second index
            for k in range(j + 1, n):                            # try every third index
                if nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0:
                    triplet = tuple(sorted([nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]]))
                    found.add(triplet)                                # a set naturally collapses duplicates
    return [list(t) for t in found]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]
    print(three_sum(nums))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every combination of three distinct indices is tried explicitly, guaranteeing no valid triplet of indices is missed.
Each qualifying triplet of values is sorted before insertion, so two different index triples producing the same values in a different order are recognized as the same triplet.
A set is relied upon entirely for deduplication, since nothing about the search order itself prevents duplicate value combinations from being found.

blocks.text: Every possible triplet of indices is checked, and the set removes any duplicate combinations of values, so this is correct.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed), for the three nested loops over every index triple.
Space: O(n) for the set of found triplets, not counting the final output.

Limitation: most of the n cubed combinations are wasted, and relying on a set of sorted triplets to catch duplicates after the fact is slower and less direct than avoiding duplicate work in the first place.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it explores every one of the n cubed index triples blindly, then leans on a set purely to paper over the duplicate triplets that blind search inevitably produces.

What sorting fixes directly: once the array is sorted, equal values sit next to each other, so a duplicate fixed value, left value, or right value is caught with one cheap adjacent comparison, no set required.

What sorting unlocks on top of that: with one value fixed, the remaining task, find two values in a sorted slice that sum to a specific target, is exactly the two pointer search already proven in Valid Palindrome.

The core idea: sort once up front, then for every fixed first value, sweep two pointers inward from both ends of the rest of the array, skipping duplicates at all three positions as they are encountered.

Sort the array first. Then fix one value at a time as the first element of a potential triplet, and use two pointers, one starting right after it and one at the very end of the array, to search for a pair that sums to the negative of the fixed value. Sorting also makes duplicate values sit next to each other, so they can be skipped directly instead of relying on a set afterward.
Sort the array, fix the first value in a loop, then use two pointers on the remainder to find pairs summing to its negation, skipping over duplicate values at every position.

blocks.caption: Optimized: sort first, fix one value, then two pointers search for the remaining pair

blocks.text: This works because sorting guarantees that for any fixed first value, the pair that sums to its negation can be found by moving the low pointer up whenever the current sum is too small and the high pointer down whenever it is too large, since sorted order means every skipped value in either direction was correctly ruled out.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the outer loop over fixed values times the two pointer scan for each one.
Space: O(log n) to O(n) depending on the sort implementation, not counting the output.

blocks.text: Sorting first turns duplicate skipping from an afterthought (a set cleaning up after the fact) into a direct, cheap check (equal to the previous value), and it enables the two pointer search that brings the complexity down from cubic to quadratic. No known algorithm solves general 3Sum faster than roughly quadratic time, so O(n squared) is considered close to optimal for this problem.

blocks.text: Mention that this is essentially "Two Sum" nested inside an outer loop, once the array has been sorted, which is a natural way to connect it to a problem the interviewer likely already discussed.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "how do you avoid duplicate triplets", think: sort first, then skip any position whose value matches the one immediately before it.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the extra set", think: sorting removes the need for a set entirely, since duplicates become adjacent.
If the interviewer says "what if we needed four numbers instead of three", think: 4Sum, fix two values in nested loops and run the same two pointer search on the rest.

Why is O(n squared) considered close to optimal for this problem, unlike Two Sum which manages O(n)?
Two Sum, whose hash map complement lookup is the pair-finding ancestor this problem builds on top of, fixing one value at a time.
Valid Palindrome, whose two pointer technique, moving inward from both ends based on a comparison, is reused directly once the array is sorted here.
Any k-sum style problem, where fixing k minus 2 values in nested loops and finishing with a two pointer search on the remainder is the standard extension of this pattern.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n cubed) time, O(n) space for deduplication. Optimized: O(n squared) time, O(log n) to O(n) space from sorting.

items: Pattern: sort the array first, then fix one value and use the two pointer technique to find the remaining pair.
Core Idea: sorting makes duplicate values adjacent, so they are cheap to skip, and it turns "find a pair summing to a target" into a two pointer scan inward from both ends of the remaining slice.
Time: O(n cubed) for the brute force, O(n squared) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) for the brute force's dedup set, O(log n) to O(n) for the optimized approach's sort.
Most Important Observation: sorting is a single decision that solves both the duplicate triplet problem and the pair search problem at the same time.
Interview Difficulty: the sort-then-two-pointer structure is standard; correctly skipping duplicates at all three positions is what separates a clean solution from a buggy one.
One line memory trick: sort, fix one, then two pointers close in on the rest.
